question: What is multi-tenancy, and what does a 'tenant' mean in your SaaS backend?
answer_hinglish:
Multi-tenancy ka matlab hai ek hi application deployment bahut saare customers ko serve karta hai, aur har customer -- yahan ek company ya organisation -- ek 'tenant' hai. Acme aur Globex dono same API, same database use karte hain, lekin Acme ka data Globex ko kabhi nahi dikhna chahiye. Yeh SaaS ka core promise hai.

Mere project mein tenant ek `tenants` table ki row hai: id, slug (jaise `acme`), name, plan aur status. User global hota hai (ek email, ek password), aur user tenants se `memberships` ke through judta hai jisme role hota hai -- owner, admin, member ya viewer. Ek user kai tenants ka member ho sakta hai, har jagah alag role ke saath. Saara tenant data -- projects, API keys, audit logs, usage counters, subscriptions, reports, invitations -- `tenant_id` column ke saath store hota hai.

Tenant-scoped routes `/t/{slug}/...` pe hain, toh URL batata hai ki request kis tenant ke context mein hai. `tenant_principal` dependency slug resolve karti hai, check karti hai ki caller us tenant ka member hai, aur ek `Principal` banati hai. Uske baad har query `tenant_tx()` ke andar chalti hai jo Postgres RLS ke liye tenant context set karta hai. Toh tenant sirf ek column nahi, poore request lifecycle ka scope hai.
why_needed: Interview ka pehla sawaal yahi hota hai; agar tenant, user aur membership ka relation clear nahi hai toh baaki sab (RLS, RBAC, plans) samjhana mushkil hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek co-working building socho: building ek hai (application), har company ka apna office (tenant) hai, ek freelancer do companies ke office ka access card rakh sakta hai (multiple memberships), lekin Acme ka card Globex ka darwaza nahi kholta.
how_it_works: User authenticate karta hai -> URL se tenant slug -> membership se role -> Principal -> tenant_tx mein queries jahan RLS sirf us tenant ki rows dikhata hai.
in_this_project: `migrations/versions/0001_initial.py` mein `tenants`, `users`, `memberships (PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, user_id))` aur baaki tenant tables hain. `POST /tenants` (`tenancy.create_tenant`) caller ko owner banata hai aur free plan deta hai. `/me` `user_tenants()` function se user ke saare workspaces dikhata hai.
code_example:
-- real (trimmed) from 0001_initial.py
CREATE TABLE memberships (
  tenant_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  user_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  role text NOT NULL CHECK (role IN ('owner', 'admin', 'member', 'viewer')),
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, user_id)
);
advantages: Ek deployment, ek migration -- operational cost kam
Users kai tenants mein ho sakte hain (realistic B2B)
disadvantages: Isolation ki zimmedari application aur DB policies pe aa jati hai
Ek tenant ka load doosron ko affect kar sakta hai
common_mistakes: User aur tenant ko same cheez maan lena (B2C soch)
Role ko users table mein rakhna -- role per tenant hota hai, global nahi

question: Compare the main multi-tenancy isolation models. Which one did you choose and why?
answer_hinglish:
Chaar main models hain. Pehla, shared database + shared schema + `tenant_id` column (pool model) -- sabse sasta, ek migration, hazaron chhote tenants ke liye perfect, lekin isolation logical hai aur noisy neighbour ka risk hai. Doosra, schema per tenant -- har tenant ka alag Postgres schema; namespace isolation milti hai aur per-tenant restore aasaan, lekin N schemas migrate karne padte hain aur hazaron schemas pe catalog bloat hota hai. Teesra, database per tenant (silo) -- physical isolation, per-tenant backup/restore trivial, noisy neighbour khatam, lekin connection pooling aur operations bahut mehenge. Chautha, hybrid -- free/pro tenants pooled, enterprise ya regulated tenants apne silo mein, beech mein ek routing layer.

Maine pool model chuna kyunki portfolio SaaS ka shape 'bahut saare chhote tenants' hai aur yeh industry ka sabse common starting point hai. Iski kamzori -- ek bhooli hui WHERE clause poora data leak kar de -- ko maine Postgres row-level security se cover kiya, aur app ko non-owner NOBYPASSRLS role se connect karaya.

SYSTEM_DESIGN.md mein table hai ki kab switch karna hai: jab koi tenant itna bada ho jaye ki uska load doosron ko hurt kare, ya compliance physical isolation maange, tab us tenant ko silo mein move karte hain -- yeh migration path hai, ek-saath poora redesign nahi.
why_needed: Tenancy model choose karna sabse pehla architecture decision hai; baaki sab (migrations, backups, scaling, security) isi pe depend karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Hostel dorm (shared room, sasta), PG mein alag kamra (schema), aur apna flat (database). Ameer client ko flat do, students ko dorm -- yeh hybrid hai.
how_it_works: Pool: har query tenant_id se filter + RLS. Schema: search_path ya schema-qualified names per tenant. DB: connection string per tenant, routing layer. Hybrid: tenant catalog batata hai tenant kis tier/cluster mein hai.
in_this_project: README aur ARCHITECTURE.md mein 'Shared database + shared schema + tenant_id column + RLS (pool model)' likha hai. SYSTEM_DESIGN.md ka 'Isolation models' table isolation, cost, noisy neighbour, per-tenant restore aur 'when' compare karta hai. Silo/hybrid is project mein implement nahi hai; woh documented scaling path hai.
advantages: Pool: sasta, ek migration, cross-tenant analytics easy
Silo: strongest isolation, easy per-tenant restore
Hybrid: pricing tiers ke saath isolation tiers
disadvantages: Pool: logical isolation, per-tenant restore mushkil
Schema/DB per tenant: N migrations, pooling pain
Hybrid: routing layer ki complexity
common_mistakes: Bina reason ke DB-per-tenant se start karna
Pool model mein sirf app-level filters pe bharosa karna
Migration path plan na karna (pool se silo kaise jayenge)

Ek tenant ko pool se silo mein bina downtime kaise move karoge?

question: What is Postgres row-level security (RLS) in simple terms?
answer_hinglish:
RLS Postgres ka feature hai jisme table pe ek policy lagti hai jo decide karti hai ki current session kaun si rows dekh, update ya insert kar sakta hai. Normal GRANT batata hai 'kya tum is table ko padh sakte ho'; RLS batata hai 'is table ki KAUN SI rows'. Postgres har query mein policy ka predicate automatically jod deta hai -- jaise ek invisible WHERE clause.

Mere project mein policy hai: `tenant_id = nullif(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid`. Har request transaction ke shuru mein `app.tenant_id` set karti hai, toh `SELECT name FROM projects` bina kisi WHERE ke bhi sirf current tenant ke projects return karta hai. Yeh `test_unfiltered_query_sees_only_current_tenant` prove karta hai: tenant A ke context mein 'a1, a2' aate hain, B ke context mein sirf 'b1'.

Important baat: RLS mera primary authorization mechanism nahi, backstop hai. App pehle se membership aur permissions check karta hai, aur sensitive lookups mein explicit tenant filter bhi lagata hai. RLS tab kaam aata hai jab developer galti kare -- WHERE bhool jaye, ya background job galat query likhe. Aur teen gotchas yaad rakhne hain: superuser aur table owner RLS bypass karte hain, context ko SET LOCAL se set karna hai, aur context na ho toh zero rows aani chahiye.
why_needed: Pool model mein ek missing WHERE clause = data breach. RLS database level pe guarantee deta hai jo code review se zyada reliable hai.
real_world_analogy: Library mein har section ke darwaaze pe guard hai jo tumhara membership card dekhkar sirf tumhare section ki books dikhata hai -- tum 'saari books do' bolo tab bhi.
how_it_works: ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY ... USING (predicate) WITH CHECK (predicate). Planner predicate ko query mein inject karta hai; index use bhi ho sakta hai.
in_this_project: `0001_initial.py` loop mein har `TENANT_TABLES` table pe ENABLE + FORCE RLS aur `tenant_isolation` policy banata hai. `tests/test_rls.py` 9 tests se SQL level pe yeh prove karta hai, bina app code ke, real `saas_app` role ke saath.
code_example:
-- real policy (0001_initial.py)
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON projects
  USING (tenant_id = nullif(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = nullif(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid);
advantages: Bhooli hui WHERE clause safe ho jati hai
Ek jagah defined, har query pe apply
Background jobs aur ad-hoc queries bhi covered
disadvantages: Debugging confusing: 'zero rows kyun?'
Superuser/owner pe kaam nahi karta
Har transaction mein context set karna padta hai
common_mistakes: App ko superuser se connect karna
RLS ko hi akela authorization maan lena
FORCE bhool jana

question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization here, and what is the Principal object?
answer_hinglish:
Authentication ka sawaal hai 'tum kaun ho?' -- yahan JWT access token ya `sk_` API key se answer milta hai. Authorization ka sawaal hai 'tum yeh kar sakte ho?' -- yeh tenant membership, role, scopes, plan aur ABAC rule se decide hota hai.

Mere project mein dono ko ek object mein combine kiya: `Principal` (core/principal.py). Yeh per request ek baar banta hai `tenant_principal` dependency mein, aur batata hai: kaun call kar raha hai (`user_id` ya `api_key_id`), kis tenant mein (`tenant_id`, `tenant_slug`), kaunse plan pe (`plan`), kaunsi permissions ke saath (`permissions` frozenset), aur audit ke liye `ip` aur `request_id`.

Routes ko token, roles, ya plans ke baare mein kuch nahi pata; woh bas `p.require(P.PROJECT_WRITE)` ya `p.require_feature('reports')` call karte hain. `require` missing permission pe 403 `forbidden` raise karta hai, `require_feature` 403 `feature_not_in_plan`. Isse authorization logic ek jagah concentrated hai aur API key aur user dono ek hi interface se handle hote hain -- API key ke liye `role` None hota hai aur permissions scopes se aati hain.

Error codes bhi alag rakhe: authentication fail = 401 `unauthorized`, authorization fail = 403, aur 'tum is tenant ke member hi nahi' = 404 (enumeration se bachne ke liye).
why_needed: Interviewers check karte hain ki aap 401 vs 403 aur identity vs permission ka fark samajhte ho, aur kya authorization ek jagah centralised hai.
real_world_analogy: Airport: passport check authentication hai (tum kaun ho), boarding pass check authorization hai (tum is flight mein, is seat pe ja sakte ho). Principal tumhara boarding pass hai.
how_it_works: Bearer token -> JWT decode ya API key resolve -> tenant + membership/scopes -> Principal(perms, plan) -> route mein require()/require_feature().
in_this_project: `saas/core/principal.py::Principal` dataclass hai with `require` aur `require_feature`. `saas/api/deps.py::tenant_principal` isse build karta hai. Error envelope `shared/bpcommon/errors.py` se aata hai: `{error: {code, message, details, request_id}}`.
advantages: User aur API key ek interface
Audit ke liye actor info ready
disadvantages: Principal request start pe freeze hota hai -- mid-request role change reflect nahi hota
Har route ko require() yaad se call karna padta hai
common_mistakes: 401 aur 403 mix karna
Route ke andar role strings compare karna instead of permissions
Non-member ko 403 dena (tenant existence leak)
follow_up_questions: Route mein require() bhool gaye toh kya bachata hai?
Permission check aur feature check alag kyun?
Principal ko cache kyun nahi karte?

question: What is a JWT, and why is your access token only valid for 15 minutes?
answer_hinglish:
JWT ek signed token hai: header, claims (payload) aur signature. Server secret se sign karta hai, aur baad mein bina database dekhe verify kar sakta hai ki token usne hi issue kiya aur claims badle nahi gaye. Isliye JWT 'stateless' hai -- har request pe sessions table hit nahi karni padti.

Mere `create_access_token` mein claims hain: `sub` (user id), `iat`, `exp`, `typ: access` aur random `jti`. Algorithm HS256 hai, secret `SAAS_JWT_SECRET` se. `decode_access_token` `algorithms=['HS256']` explicitly deta hai (algorithm confusion attack se bachav), `exp`, `sub`, `typ` ko required banata hai, aur `typ != 'access'` pe reject karta hai.

15 minute kyun? Stateless ka nuksaan yeh hai ki token expiry se pehle revoke nahi ho sakta -- logout ke baad bhi chori hua access token valid rehta hai. TTL chhota rakhke yeh window 15 minute tak limit hoti hai. Lambi sessions ke liye refresh token hai jo DB mein stored, hashed, single-use aur revocable hai. Plus, tenant routes pe membership har request check hoti hai (cache 60s TTL + invalidation), toh member ko tenant se hatane ka asar turant hota hai, chahe JWT valid ho. TRADEOFFS.md #5 yahi baat likhta hai. Revocation window SECURITY.md mein documented gap hai.
why_needed: Token-based auth har backend interview mein aata hai; TTL aur revocation ka trade-off samajhna zaroori hai.
real_world_analogy: Cinema ka ticket: gate pe sirf stamp check hota hai (signature), counter pe call nahi karte. Lekin ticket chori ho gaya toh show khatam hone tak valid -- isliye show chhota rakho.
how_it_works: Header.Payload base64url + HMAC-SHA256(secret) signature. Verify: signature recompute, exp check, required claims check.
in_this_project: `saas/core/security.py::create_access_token` aur `decode_access_token`. `config.py` mein `access_token_ttl_seconds: int = 900`. `deps.py::current_user_id` user-only routes ke liye JWT verify karta hai aur API key ko reject karta hai.
advantages: No DB hit per request for auth
Horizontal scaling easy -- koi session store nahi
Chhota TTL leak window limit karta hai
disadvantages: Expiry se pehle revoke nahi
Secret leak = koi bhi token mint kar sakta hai
HS256 mein verify karne wale ko bhi sign karne ki power
common_mistakes: algorithms list na dena
Lamba TTL (din bhar) rakhna
JWT mein role/permissions daalna jo stale ho jayein
follow_up_questions: Token ko expiry se pehle revoke kaise karoge?

question: Why do you hash passwords with bcrypt but refresh tokens, invitation tokens and API keys with plain SHA-256?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki dono ka threat model alag hai. Password human-chosen hota hai -- low entropy, dictionary words, reuse. Agar DB leak ho jaye toh attacker offline guess karega: 'password123', 'acme2026'... Isliye password hash slow aur salted hona chahiye. bcrypt deliberately mehenga hai (cost 12 = 2^12 rounds), har hash ka random salt hai, toh har guess costly hai aur rainbow tables bekaar.

Tokens aur API keys ka case alag hai. `opaque_token` `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` use karta hai -- 32 random bytes, 256 bits entropy. Iska koi dictionary nahi; brute force practically impossible hai chahe hash fast ho. Toh slow hash ka koi security fayda nahi, aur nuksaan bada hai: bcrypt salted hai, toh same input ka hash har baar alag -- tum `WHERE key_hash = :h` se index lookup nahi kar sakte. SHA-256 deterministic hai, toh `api_keys.key_hash UNIQUE` aur `refresh_tokens.token_hash UNIQUE` pe O(log n) B-tree lookup hota hai. Aur har API request pe bcrypt (~100s of ms at cost 12, typically) chalana latency maar dega.

`security.py` ka docstring yahi likhta hai: 'Long random tokens don't need bcrypt (no dictionary to brute force); SHA-256 allows indexed lookup.' Dono cases mein raw value DB mein kabhi nahi hoti -- DB leak se tokens use nahi ho sakte.
why_needed: Yeh classic 'kab slow hash, kab fast hash' sawaal hai; galat answer (har cheez bcrypt) performance aur design dono ki samajh ki kami dikhata hai.
real_world_analogy: Ghar ki chaabi (password) simple ho sakti hai isliye mazboot tijori (bcrypt) chahiye; bank locker ka 40-digit random code (API key) khud hi itna strong hai ki simple register mein likh ke rakh sakte ho -- bas original nahi, uska fingerprint.
how_it_works: bcrypt: salt + cost factor, verify by recomputing. SHA-256: deterministic digest, unique index pe equality lookup.
in_this_project: `hash_password` `bcrypt.gensalt(rounds)` (config `bcrypt_rounds = 12`, tests mein 4) use karta hai. `sha256()` tokens ke liye; `create_api_key` `sha256(raw)` store karta hai aur raw sirf ek baar return karta hai. Passwords 10-72 chars validate hote hain kyunki bcrypt 72 bytes ke baad ignore karta hai.
advantages: DB leak se raw tokens nahi milte
disadvantages: SHA-256 sirf high-entropy secrets ke liye safe hai
Short/user-chosen secrets ke liye galat choice
common_mistakes: API keys ko bcrypt karna aur phir har key pe loop karke compare karna
Passwords ko SHA-256 karna
72-byte bcrypt limit ignore karna

question: What is a subscription plan and an entitlement, and how is a rate limit different from a quota?
answer_hinglish:
Plan ek product tier hai (free, pro, enterprise) aur entitlement woh cheez hai jo plan tumhe allow karta hai -- limits (kitne projects, kitne members) aur features (reports, audit_export, sso). Mere `core/plans.py` mein `Plan` frozen dataclass hai: `max_projects`, `max_members`, `features`, `requests_per_second`, `burst`, `monthly_api_calls`. Free: 3 projects, 3 members, sirf 'projects' feature, 5 rps, burst 10, 10,000 calls per month. Pro: 50 projects, 25 members, reports + audit_export, 50 rps, 1,000,000 calls. Enterprise: unlimited (None) aur 'sso' flag.

Rate limit aur quota alag problems solve karte hain. Rate limit short window (per second) hai -- burst ko smooth karna aur noisy neighbour ko rokna; yeh Redis token bucket se `saas:rl:{tenant}` key pe hota hai aur 429 `rate_limited` + `Retry-After` deta hai. Quota long window (per month) hai -- commercial limit, 'tumne plan ke paise jitne calls kharide'; yeh `saas:usage:{tenant}:api_calls:{YYYY-MM}` counter pe INCR hai aur 429 `quota_exceeded` deta hai. Retry-After quota ke liye meaningless hai -- agle mahine ya upgrade tak block.

Teesri cheez: limits jaise max_projects 403 `plan_limit_reached` dete hain, aur missing feature 403 `feature_not_in_plan`. Har failure ka distinct code hai taaki client aur sales dono samjhein kya hua -- DEPLOYMENT.md inhe 'upsell signal' bhi kehta hai.
why_needed: SaaS backend ka business side yahi hai; interviewer dekhta hai ki aap 'technical limit' aur 'commercial limit' ka fark samajhte ho.
real_world_analogy: Mobile plan: 'speed 50 Mbps' rate limit hai, '2 GB per day' quota hai, aur 'international roaming included' feature/entitlement hai.
how_it_works: Request -> check_rate (token bucket) -> meter (INCR, compare quota) -> route mein require_feature / count-under-lock for limits.
in_this_project: `saas/core/plans.py::PLANS` dict, `get_plan` unknown name pe free return karta hai. `services/limits.py::TenantLimits.check_rate` aur `meter`. `services/errors.py` mein `PlanLimitReached`, `FeatureNotInPlan`, `QuotaExceeded`. Test: `test_tenant_rate_limit_and_quota`, `test_plan_entitlements_and_upgrade_via_billing_webhook`.
advantages: Distinct error codes -> clear client behaviour
Plans code review se guzarte hain
Rate aur quota alag tune ho sakte hain
disadvantages: Per-tenant custom deals ke liye overrides table nahi hai
Downgrade pe over-limit data delete nahi hota
common_mistakes: Rate limit aur quota ko ek hi counter se karna

Feature flags ko role permissions mein mix karna

question: What is the difference between ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY?
answer_hinglish:
`ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` table pe RLS on karta hai -- lekin by default yeh table ke OWNER pe apply nahi hota (aur superusers ya BYPASSRLS roles pe kabhi nahi). Owner ko Postgres trusted maanta hai. `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` kehta hai ki policies table owner pe bhi lagengi.

Mere migration mein dono hain: loop har `TENANT_TABLES` table pe `ENABLE` aur `FORCE` chalata hai, comment ke saath 'applies even to the table owner'. Kyun dono? Primary defence yeh hai ki app owner hi nahi hai -- tables owner role (migrations wala `bp`/`owner`) ke hain aur app `saas_app` se connect karta hai. FORCE ek extra safety net hai: agar kabhi koi galti se app ko owner URL se chala de, ya owner role se maintenance script tenant context ke saath chale, tab bhi policies apply hon.

Lekin ek important limit hai: FORCE superuser pe kaam nahi karta. Superuser aur `BYPASSRLS` attribute wale roles RLS ko completely ignore karte hain. `test_superuser_would_bypass_rls` exactly yeh demonstrate karta hai -- tests ka owner URL (`bp`) superuser hai, aur random tenant context ke saath bhi `count(*)` 3 aata hai, yaani sab rows. Isliye DEPLOYMENT.md kehta hai: 'Never point the app at the owner/superuser URL: RLS would silently stop protecting anything.' Aur `saas_app` explicitly `NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS` banaya gaya hai.
why_needed: Sabse common RLS gotcha yahi hai -- log policy likh dete hain, owner se test karte hain, sab rows dikhti hain, aur confuse hote hain (ya worse, production mein owner se connect karte hain).
real_world_analogy: Building ka rule 'sab ID dikhayenge' -- ENABLE ke baad bhi building ka maalik bina ID ghus sakta hai; FORCE maalik ko bhi ID dikhane pe majboor karta hai; lekin police commissioner (superuser) pe koi rule nahi chalta.
how_it_works: Policy check skip hota hai agar: role superuser hai, ya BYPASSRLS hai, ya role table owner hai AUR table FORCE nahi hai.
in_this_project: `migrations/versions/0001_initial.py` mein `for t in TENANT_TABLES: ... ENABLE ... FORCE`. `CREATE ROLE saas_app LOGIN ... NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS`. Test `tests/test_rls.py::test_superuser_would_bypass_rls`.
code_example:
# real 0001_initial.py
for t in TENANT_TABLES:
    op.execute(f"ALTER TABLE {t} ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY")
    op.execute(f"ALTER TABLE {t} FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY")   # applies even to the table owner
advantages: Owner galti se use ho tab bhi policies lagti hain
disadvantages: Superuser pe phir bhi bypass
Owner se maintenance scripts ko bhi tenant context chahiye

Superuser se app chalana

question: Explain USING versus WITH CHECK in an RLS policy, with examples from your tests.
answer_hinglish:
`USING` existing rows pe lagta hai -- SELECT kaunsi rows dekh sakta hai, aur UPDATE/DELETE kaunsi rows ko target kar sakte hain. `WITH CHECK` nayi ya badli hui rows pe lagta hai -- INSERT ki row aur UPDATE ke baad wali row policy pass karni chahiye, warna error. Simple yaad: USING = 'kya dikh sakta hai', WITH CHECK = 'kya likh sakta hai'.

Mere policies dono mein same predicate use karti hain: `tenant_id = nullif(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid`. Ab teen tests dekho. `test_cannot_write_into_another_tenant`: tenant A ke context mein `INSERT ... VALUES (:b_tenant, 'evil')` -- WITH CHECK fail, Postgres 'new row violates row-level security policy' error deta hai. `test_cannot_update_or_delete_other_tenants_rows`: A ke context mein `UPDATE projects SET name='pwned' WHERE tenant_id = :b` -- koi error nahi, bas rowcount 0, kyunki USING ne B ki rows invisible kar di. Aur `DELETE FROM projects` (bina WHERE!) sirf A ki 2 rows delete karta hai.

Notice karo behaviour ka fark: invisible rows pe UPDATE/DELETE silently 0 rows, jabki galat INSERT loud error. Agar WITH CHECK na hota toh tenant A ek row ka tenant_id B mein badal ke data 'push' kar sakta tha. Jab WITH CHECK omit karo toh Postgres USING expression ko hi check ke liye use karta hai, lekin explicitly likhna clearer hai -- aur 0001 ke original memberships policy mein USING aur CHECK alag the, wahi bug ka source bana.
why_needed: Interviewers USING/WITH CHECK ka fark poochte hain kyunki yeh batata hai ki aap write-path isolation ke baare mein soche ho ya sirf read leakage.
real_world_analogy: USING = kaunse almari ke darwaaze tum khol sakte ho; WITH CHECK = tum kis almari mein naya saamaan rakh sakte ho. Dono pe alag lock.
how_it_works: SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE: USING filter rows. INSERT: WITH CHECK new row. UPDATE: USING old row + WITH CHECK new row.
in_this_project: Policies `0001_initial.py` aur `0003_strict_memberships_policy.py` mein. Tests: `test_cannot_write_into_another_tenant` (pytest.raises DBAPIError match 'row-level security'), `test_cannot_update_or_delete_other_tenants_rows` (upd.rowcount == 0, dele.rowcount == 2).
code_example:
# real (trimmed) tests/test_rls.py
async with tenant_tx(sm, a) as s:
    upd = await s.execute(text("UPDATE projects SET name = 'pwned' WHERE tenant_id = :b"), {"b": b})
    dele = await s.execute(text("DELETE FROM projects"))
    assert upd.rowcount == 0 and dele.rowcount == 2   # only A's own rows were affected
advantages: Read aur write dono paths covered

question: Why does your policy use current_setting('app.tenant_id', true) wrapped in nullif, and what does 'fail closed' mean?
answer_hinglish:
`current_setting(name)` ek custom GUC (configuration variable) padhta hai. Agar variable set hi nahi hai toh default form error throw karta hai: 'unrecognized configuration parameter'. Doosra argument `true` matlab `missing_ok` -- set nahi hai toh error ke bajaye NULL return karo. Policy mein error hum nahi chahte kyunki `global_tx` jaisi legitimate queries (users, tenants) bhi tenant tables touch kar sakti hain.

`nullif(..., '')` kyun? Postgres ki ek subtlety: ek baar transaction mein `set_config` local set ho chuka ho, toh transaction ke baad us session mein variable 'exist' karta hai lekin value empty string '' ho jati hai, NULL nahi. Aur mera `tenant_tx` khud bhi tenant na ho toh `''` set karta hai. `''::uuid` cast error deta. `nullif` empty string ko NULL mein convert karta hai.

Ab 'fail closed': `tenant_id = NULL` SQL mein NULL hai, TRUE nahi, toh koi row match nahi karti. Matlab context missing = zero rows, sab rows nahi. Fail open hota toh missing context = poora database. `test_no_tenant_context_sees_nothing` `global_tx` mein `SELECT count(*) FROM projects` chalata hai aur 0 expect karta hai, aur `test_context_does_not_leak_between_transactions` bhi check karta hai ki naye transaction mein `current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)` `None` ya `''` hai. Security mein default hamesha deny hona chahiye -- bug ka result 'empty page' ho, 'data breach' nahi.
why_needed: Yeh detail dikhati hai ki aapne RLS sach mein production mein chalaya hai; '' vs NULL ki subtlety sirf tab pata chalti hai jab cheez toot-ti hai.
real_world_analogy: Electronic door lock jo power cut pe LOCKED rehta hai (fail closed) vs jo khul jaata hai (fail open). Bank vault ka lock hamesha fail closed.
how_it_works: Unset -> missing_ok NULL; set-then-ended -> ''; nullif('') -> NULL; tenant_id = NULL -> NULL -> row filtered out.
in_this_project: Policy text `0001_initial.py` aur `0003_*` mein. `db/session.py::tenant_tx` tenant None hone pe `''` pass karta hai, aur `global_tx` wahi call karta hai. Comment 0001 mein: 'So a request that forgot to set the tenant sees NOTHING (fail closed), not everything.'
code_example:
-- illustrative psql session
SELECT current_setting('app.tenant_id', true);         -- NULL (never set)
BEGIN; SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', 'abc', true); COMMIT;
SELECT current_setting('app.tenant_id', true);         -- '' (exists, empty)
SELECT nullif(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid;  -- NULL, no cast error
advantages: Missing context ka result empty, not breach
disadvantages: 'Zero rows' bug debug karna confusing
Policy expression thoda verbose
common_mistakes: current_setting bina missing_ok ke -- global queries error karengi
nullif bhoolna -- ''::uuid cast error
Default tenant ya 'all' fallback rakhna

Custom GUC naam mein dot kyun chahiye (app.tenant_id)?
Is predicate pe index use hota hai kya?

question: Why set the tenant context with SET LOCAL (set_config(..., true)) instead of SET, and how does that interact with connection pools?
answer_hinglish:
`SET` session-scoped hai -- value connection pe tab tak rehti hai jab tak connection band na ho ya reset na ho. `SET LOCAL` transaction-scoped hai -- COMMIT ya ROLLBACK pe automatically khatam. `set_config(name, value, true)` ka teesra argument `is_local` hai, toh yeh SET LOCAL ka function form hai.

Connection pool mein ek physical connection kai requests mein reuse hota hai. Agar request 1 (Acme) ne plain `SET app.tenant_id = acme` kiya aur connection pool mein wapas gaya, toh request 2 (Globex user) ko wahi connection mila aur agar kisi code path ne naya context set karna miss kar diya -- woh Acme ka data dekhega. Cross-tenant leak, aur woh bhi intermittent, debug karna nightmare. SET LOCAL ke saath transaction khatam = context khatam, toh agla borrower clean slate pe start karta hai aur fail-closed policy zero rows deti hai.

Function form kyun, `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = '...'` kyun nahi? Kyunki `SET` statement mein bind parameters nahi chalte -- string interpolate karna padta, jo SQL injection ka darwaza hai. `SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', :t, true)` fully parameterised hai. SECURITY.md isko explicitly list karta hai.

Trade-off: har tenant query transaction ke andar honi chahiye, aur PgBouncer transaction mode ke saath yeh perfectly compatible hai (session SET nahi hai). `test_context_does_not_leak_between_transactions` same pool pe naya transaction kholta hai aur verify karta hai ki setting empty hai aur count 0.
why_needed: Pooled connections pe session state leak sabse sneaky multi-tenant bug hai; interviewers yeh specifically poochte hain.
real_world_analogy: Hotel room: SET LOCAL checkout pe room ki saafai hai; SET waisa hai jaise pichhle guest ka saamaan room mein chhod do aur agla guest use kar le.
how_it_works: BEGIN -> set_config(..., true) -> queries -> COMMIT/ROLLBACK -> GUC revert. Pool connection return karta hai bina tenant state ke.
in_this_project: `saas/db/session.py::tenant_tx` -- `async with sm() as s, s.begin(): await s.execute(text("SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', :t, true), set_config('app.user_id', :u, true)"), ...)`. Engine `pool_size=10, max_overflow=10, pool_pre_ping=True`. DEPLOYMENT.md: 'PgBouncer in transaction mode is compatible (SET LOCAL)'.
code_example:
# real db/session.py
@contextlib.asynccontextmanager
async def tenant_tx(sm, tenant_id, user_id=None):
    async with sm() as s, s.begin():
        # set_config(name, value, is_local=true) == SET LOCAL, but parameterised (no SQL injection).
        await s.execute(text("SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', :t, true), set_config('app.user_id', :u, true)"),
                        {"t": str(tenant_id) if tenant_id else "", "u": str(user_id) if user_id else ""})
        yield s
disadvantages: Har tenant query ko transaction chahiye
Ek extra statement per transaction (round trip)
common_mistakes: Plain SET use karna
f-string se SET LOCAL banana
Autocommit mode mein set_config(..., true) chalana -- turant khatam ho jaata hai

PgBouncer statement mode ke saath kya hoga?
Set_config ko query ke saath ek round trip mein kaise merge karoge?

question: Why must the application connect as a dedicated NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS role that does not own the tables?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki Postgres mein teen tarah ke roles RLS se bach jaate hain: superusers (hamesha), `BYPASSRLS` attribute wale roles (hamesha), aur table owner (jab tak FORCE na ho). Agar app inmein se kisi role se connect kare toh saari policies silently kuch nahi karengi -- koi error nahi, bas sab data dikhega. Yeh sabse khatarnak failure mode hai kyunki sab kaam karta hua lagta hai.

Isliye project mein do database identities hain (DEPLOYMENT.md). Owner role (`SAAS_MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL`) sirf `alembic upgrade head` ke liye -- tables own karta hai, role/policies/functions banata hai. App role `saas_app` (`SAAS_DATABASE_URL`) -- migration 0001 `CREATE ROLE saas_app LOGIN PASSWORD ... NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS` se banata hai, aur sirf DML grants deta hai; audit_logs pe sirf SELECT, INSERT. `migrations/env.py` ka docstring: 'Migrations run as the OWNER role, never as the app role.' `config.py` comment bhi yahi warning deta hai.

Tests bhi real `saas_app` se connect karte hain (`APP_URL`), owner sirf TRUNCATE ke liye -- isliye RLS tests meaningful hain. Aur `test_superuser_would_bypass_rls` negative demonstration hai: owner URL se random tenant context ke saath bhi 3 rows dikhti hain.

Least privilege ka bonus: app compromise ho jaye toh bhi woh DDL nahi chala sakta, policies drop nahi kar sakta, audit log edit nahi kar sakta.
why_needed: RLS ka sabse bada real-world failure 'app superuser se connected tha' hai. Separate roles dikhata hai ki aap least privilege samajhte ho.
real_world_analogy: Bank ka manager (owner) vault ke rules banata hai, lekin counter pe baitha cashier (app role) sirf apne counter ke drawer khol sakta hai; agar cashier ko manager ki chaabi de do toh saare rules bekaar.
how_it_works: Role attributes: rolsuper, rolbypassrls. Ownership: pg_class.relowner. App role ke paas sirf GRANTed privileges; policies enforce.
in_this_project: `0001_initial.py` role creation + GRANT block. `docker-compose.yml` x-env mein dono URLs; `migrate` service owner se, `api` aur `worker` saas_app se. `tests/conftest.py` mein `APP_URL` vs `OWNER_URL`.
advantages: Compromised app DDL/audit tamper nahi kar sakta
disadvantages: Do credentials manage karne padte hain
Migration aur app deploy alag steps
common_mistakes: Dev convenience ke liye app ko postgres superuser se chalana
Migrations app role se chalana (phir app owner ban jaata hai)
Managed DB ke default admin user ko app mein use karna

Read replica pe bhi yahi role chahiye?

advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar deploy config galti se owner URL app ko de de, toh koi test fail nahi hoga production mein -- sab kaam karega, isolation gayab. Isliye startup check chahiye.
advanced.alternatives: Application-only filtering (no RLS); ya schema/DB per tenant jahan isolation connection level pe hai; ya views with security_barrier.

question: What are SECURITY DEFINER functions, why does this project need resolve_api_key, accept_invitation_lookup and user_tenants, and what are the risks?
answer_hinglish:
Normal function caller ke privileges se chalta hai (SECURITY INVOKER). `SECURITY DEFINER` function apne OWNER ke privileges se chalta hai -- jaise Unix setuid. Yahan owner migration role hai jo superuser hai, toh function ke andar RLS lagta hi nahi.

Kyun chahiye? Teen flows mein tenant pehle se pata nahi hota, aur strict RLS row chhupa deta. (1) API key auth: request mein sirf `sk_...` hai; key kis tenant ki hai woh key row se hi pata chalega -- `resolve_api_key(p_hash)`. (2) Invitation accept: token se tenant milta hai -- `accept_invitation_lookup(p_hash)` (migration 0002). (3) 'Mere workspaces' (`/me`): ek user ke saare tenants -- `user_tenants(p_user)` (migration 0003). Har function narrow hai: exact hash/user id pe lookup, sirf zaroori columns return, extra filters (`revoked_at IS NULL`, `accepted_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now()`).

Risks: function RLS ka official bypass hai, toh isme bug = cross-tenant leak. Specific risks: (a) search_path hijack -- attacker apna schema aage rakh ke `api_keys` naam ki table/function inject kare; isliye har function `SET search_path = public` karta hai. (b) Broad access -- `REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC` aur sirf `saas_app` ko EXECUTE. (c) Input jo caller control karta hai -- `user_tenants(p_user)` caller jo bhi uuid de uske workspaces de dega; yeh sirf isliye safe hai ki app `user_id` JWT se pass karta hai, client se nahi. Yeh trust boundary yaad rakhni chahiye.
why_needed: Har serious RLS deployment ko kahin na kahin cross-tenant lookup chahiye; interviewer dekhta hai ki aap bypass ko narrow aur audited rakhte ho ya policy mein OR daal dete ho.
real_world_analogy: Building mein ek reception desk jahan guard (definer) master key rakhta hai, lekin sirf ek kaam karta hai: 'is token number ka parcel kis floor ka hai' batana -- poori building ki chaabi visitor ko nahi deta.
how_it_works: CREATE FUNCTION ... LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public AS $$ SELECT ... WHERE key_hash = p_hash $$; REVOKE ALL FROM PUBLIC; GRANT EXECUTE TO saas_app.
in_this_project: `resolve_api_key` 0001 mein, `accept_invitation_lookup` 0002 mein, `user_tenants` 0003 mein. Callers: `deps.tenant_principal`, `tenancy.accept_invitation`, `tenancy.my_tenants`. Test: `test_api_key_resolution_via_security_definer` -- `SELECT count(*) FROM api_keys` 0 deta hai (RLS), lekin function exact hash se row deta hai.

-- real 0001_initial.py
CREATE FUNCTION resolve_api_key(p_hash text)
RETURNS TABLE (key_id uuid, tenant_id uuid, scopes text[], created_by uuid)
LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public AS $$
  SELECT id, tenant_id, scopes, created_by FROM api_keys WHERE key_hash = p_hash AND revoked_at IS NULL
$$;
REVOKE ALL ON FUNCTION resolve_api_key(text) FROM PUBLIC;
advantages: Policies strict reh sakti hain (no OR)
disadvantages: Function bug = RLS bypass
Owner superuser hai -- function mein jo bhi ho, full power
Caller-controlled input pe trust
common_mistakes: search_path set na karna
SELECT * return karna (password_hash jaise columns)
EXECUTE ko PUBLIC pe chhod dena
Function ko generic 'run query for tenant X' bana dena
follow_up_questions: user_tenants ko caller ka user id khud kaise lene doge bina parameter ke?
Function owner ko superuser ki jagah dedicated role kyun banana chahiye?
In functions ko review/test kaise karte ho?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Policy mein OR (simple, lekin invariant todta hai) vs SECURITY DEFINER functions (thoda zyada code, bypass explicit). Maine functions chune aur 0003 ne OR hata diya.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar function filter galat ho (jaise revoked_at check bhoolna) toh revoked keys kaam karengi; agar parameter client se aaye toh enumeration. search_path bhoolne pe function hijack.
advanced.alternatives: Ek alag 'auth' schema/table jo tenant-scoped nahi (global key index: hash -> tenant_id); ya BYPASSRLS wala dedicated auth service role; ya user_id ko current_setting('app.user_id') se function ke andar padhna instead of parameter.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Lookup functions hot path pe hain (har API key request) -- unique index pe O(log n) hai toh scale theek hai; 100x pe result Redis mein short TTL ke saath cache karo with revoke-invalidation.

question: What is the difference between RBAC and ABAC, using your project-delete rule as the example?
answer_hinglish:
RBAC (role-based access control) poochta hai 'is ROLE ko kya karne ki ijazat hai?'. Mere `core/rbac.py` mein chaar roles hain jo nested sets hain: viewer (project:read, member:read), member (+ project:write, report:run), admin (+ project:delete, member:invite, member:manage, apikey:manage, audit:read), owner (+ billing:manage, tenant:manage). `ROLE_PERMISSIONS` dict role ko frozenset of `P` enum mein map karta hai.

ABAC (attribute-based) user, resource aur context ke attributes pe decide karta hai. Example: 'member apna BANAYA HUA project delete kar sakta hai, doosre ka nahi'. Yeh RBAC se express nahi hota -- agar member ko `project:delete` do toh woh sabke projects delete karega; na do toh apna bhi nahi. Resource ka attribute (`created_by`) chahiye.

`can_delete_project(permissions, actor_user_id, project_created_by)` dono ko combine karta hai: agar `PROJECT_DELETE` hai (admin/owner) toh true; warna `PROJECT_WRITE` hai AUR actor hi creator hai toh true. `PROJECT_WRITE` wali condition viewer ko bahar rakhti hai, aur `actor_user_id is not None` API keys (jinka user_id None hai) ko creator rule se bahar rakhta hai.

`test_rbac_and_abac` prove karta hai: member owner ka project delete kare -> 403, apna -> 204; viewer project create kare -> 403. TRADEOFFS.md #6: zyada rules aayein toh OPA/Cedar jaisa policy engine next step hai.
why_needed: Har SaaS mein 'apna resource' type rules aate hain; interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki aap RBAC ki limit pehchante ho.
real_world_analogy: Office mein manager (role) kisi ka bhi leave approve kar sakta hai -- RBAC. Lekin 'tum apni hi expense report edit kar sakte ho' -- yeh attribute (report kiski hai) pe depend karta hai -- ABAC.
how_it_works: Permission check: role -> perms set. ABAC check: perms + (actor == resource.created_by). Route pe pehle resource load, phir rule.
in_this_project: `saas/core/rbac.py::can_delete_project`, `ROLE_PERMISSIONS`. `tenancy.delete_project` pehle `get_project` (RLS + 404) karta hai phir rule check. SECURITY.md mein permission matrix table.

disadvantages: ABAC rules code mein bikhar sakte hain
Custom roles per tenant support nahi

ABAC check se pehle resource tenant-scoped load na karna
None == None compare se API key ko creator maan lena

question: How does refresh-token rotation with reuse detection work, and why revoke the whole family?
answer_hinglish:
Access token 15 minute ka hai, toh client ko lambi session ke liye refresh token chahiye. Mera refresh token opaque random string hai (`rt_` + 32 bytes), DB mein sirf sha256 hash stored, 30 din ka TTL, aur SINGLE USE. Har `/auth/refresh` pe: purana token revoke (`revoked_at = now()`, `replaced_by = new_id`) aur naya pair issue -- same `family_id` ke saath. Family = ek login session ki poori chain.

Reuse detection: agar koi ALREADY-revoked token dobara aata hai, iska matlab do log same token chain use kar rahe hain -- yaani chori. Hum nahi jaante kaun attacker hai aur kaun victim (dono ke paas valid looking token tha), toh safe answer: poori family revoke -- `UPDATE refresh_tokens SET revoked_at = coalesce(revoked_at, now()) WHERE family_id = :f`. Attacker aur victim dono logout; victim dobara login karega toh nayi family banegi, attacker ke paas kuch nahi bachega.

Ek subtle point: family revoke karke hum `Unauthorized` raise karte hain. Exception se transaction rollback ho jaata aur revocation bhi undo ho jaati! Isliye code explicitly `await s.commit()` karta hai raise se pehle -- comment: 'keep the family revocation even though we raise'. Aur lookup `FOR UPDATE` ke saath hai taaki do concurrent refreshes same token pe race na karein.

`test_auth_flow_and_refresh_rotation_with_reuse_detection` exact scenario chalata hai: refresh -> r1; purana token replay -> 401 'reuse'; ab r1 bhi 401.
why_needed: OAuth best practice (refresh token rotation) hai; interviewer reuse detection ka reasoning aur commit-before-raise jaisi subtlety dekhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek building pass jo har entry pe naya milta hai aur purana punch ho jaata hai. Agar koi punched pass leke aaye, toh security us pass ki poori chain (tumhara aur jo bhi uske baad bana) cancel karke dono ko reception bhej deti hai.
how_it_works: refresh(token): SELECT ... FOR UPDATE by hash -> missing/expired 401 -> revoked? revoke family + commit + 401 -> else issue new (same family) + revoke old.
in_this_project: `saas/services/auth.py::AuthService.refresh`, `_issue`, `logout` (poori family revoke). Table `refresh_tokens (family_id, token_hash UNIQUE, revoked_at, replaced_by)` + `ix_refresh_family`.
code_example:
# real (trimmed) services/auth.py
row = (await s.execute(text(
    "SELECT id, user_id, family_id, expires_at, revoked_at FROM refresh_tokens WHERE token_hash = :h FOR UPDATE"),
    {"h": sha256(token)})).first()
if row.revoked_at is not None:
    await s.execute(text("UPDATE refresh_tokens SET revoked_at = coalesce(revoked_at, now()) WHERE family_id = :f"),
                    {"f": row.family_id})
    await s.commit()   # keep the family revocation even though we raise
    raise Unauthorized("refresh token reuse detected; all sessions in this family revoked")
advantages: Chori hua refresh token detect hota hai
disadvantages: Network retry (client ne response miss kiya aur purana bheja) bhi family revoke kar deta hai -- false positive
Access token phir bhi 15 min valid

Rotation bina reuse detection ke (chori ka pata hi nahi chalega)

question: What does it mean for webhook processing to be idempotent, and how does billing_events make it so?
answer_hinglish:
Idempotent matlab same operation ko ek baar karo ya das baar, result same. Billing providers (Stripe, Razorpay) webhooks 'at-least-once' deliver karte hain -- network timeout, hamara 500, ya unka retry logic -- toh same event `subscription.updated` do ya zyada baar aa sakta hai. Agar har delivery ko naya event maano toh side effects double ho sakte hain: double audit row, double credit, ya purana event naye state ko overwrite kare.

Mera solution simple aur database-enforced hai: `billing_events` table jiska `id` provider ka event id hai aur PRIMARY KEY hai. `apply_event` sabse pehle `INSERT INTO billing_events (id, type, payload)` karta hai. Agar event pehle aa chuka hai toh PK violation -> `IntegrityError` -> function `False` return karta hai aur kuch apply nahi hota. Route `{received: true, duplicate: true}` 200 ke saath return karta hai -- 200 zaroori hai, warna provider retry karta rahega.

Kyun 'check then insert' nahi (`SELECT ... if not exists`)? Kyunki do concurrent deliveries dono check pass kar sakti hain. Unique constraint pe insert atomic hai -- database guarantee karta hai sirf ek jeetega.

`test_plan_entitlements_and_upgrade_via_billing_webhook` same body aur valid signature dobara bhejta hai aur `duplicate is True` assert karta hai. Note: `billing_events` tenant-scoped nahi (no RLS) kyunki event aane ke waqt tenant pata nahi hota -- migration ka comment yahi kehta hai.
why_needed: Webhooks, payments, queues -- har distributed integration mein idempotency core concept hai.
real_world_analogy: Courier ka parcel tracking number: godown pe register mein number pehle se likha hai toh dobara entry nahi karte, chahe courier wala do baar aa jaye.
how_it_works: INSERT event id (PK) -> success: apply side effects -> commit. Conflict: return duplicate, 200 OK.
in_this_project: `saas/services/billing.py::apply_event`; table `billing_events (id text PRIMARY KEY, type, payload jsonb, processed_at)` 0001 mein. Route `api/routes.py::billing_webhook` `{received, duplicate}` return karta hai.

    try:
        await s.execute(text("INSERT INTO billing_events (id, type, payload) VALUES (:i, :t, CAST(:p AS jsonb))"),
                        {"i": evt.id, "t": evt.type, "p": raw.decode()})
    except IntegrityError:
        return False
    ...

question: Walk through tenant_principal step by step. What happens, in what order, for a request to /t/acme/projects?
answer_hinglish:
`tenant_principal` har `/t/{slug}` route ki FastAPI dependency hai aur yahi poore authorization pipeline ka dil hai. Order: (1) `_tenant_by_slug` -- `global_tx` mein `SELECT id, slug, name, plan, status FROM tenants WHERE slug = :s`, result `TenantCache` mein `_global` namespace pe `tenant-slug:{slug}` key se cached; na mile toh 404. (2) `_bearer` header se token nikalta hai, missing pe 401. (3a) Token `sk_` se shuru -> API key path: `resolve_api_key(sha256(token))`; nahi mila -> 401; key ka tenant URL tenant se alag -> 404 (enumeration); phir `tenant_tx` mein creator ka current role; permissions = scopes AND role permissions. (3b) Warna JWT path: `decode_access_token`; phir `tenant_tx(tid, user_id)` mein `SELECT role FROM memberships WHERE tenant_id = :t AND user_id = :u`, cached as `member-role:{user_id}` in the tenant namespace; role None -> 404. (4) Suspension: status 'suspended' -> 403. (5) `ip` aur `request_id` attach. (6) `check_rate` -> 429 rate_limited. (7) `meter` -> 429 quota_exceeded. (8) Principal return.

Order ke implications: suspended tenant ki requests metering tak nahi pahunchti (test comment: 'suspended calls are rejected before metering'). Rate-limited requests meter nahi hoti. Fix: `tenant_principal` ab pehle token/API key validate karta hai, phir tenant resolve (`test_no_tenant_enumeration_without_valid_credentials`).

question: How is tenant_tx implemented, and how do global_tx and tenant_tx differ?
answer_hinglish:
`tenant_tx(sm, tenant_id, user_id=None)` ek async context manager hai. Woh session kholta hai, `s.begin()` se transaction start karta hai, aur pehla statement `SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', :t, true), set_config('app.user_id', :u, true)` chalata hai -- dono settings transaction-local. Phir session caller ko yield hota hai; block normally khatam ho toh COMMIT, exception pe ROLLBACK -- `s.begin()` context manager yeh handle karta hai. Agar tenant_id None hai toh value `''` set hoti hai.

`global_tx(sm, user_id=None)` bas `tenant_tx(sm, None, user_id)` hai. Matlab: koi tenant context nahi, toh har RLS-protected table zero rows dega (fail closed). Yeh users, tenants, refresh_tokens, billing_events jaise non-tenant tables ke liye hai -- login, registration, tenant slug lookup, admin tenant list.

Design choice: caller ko kabhi raw session nahi milta bina context ke -- tenant data chahiye toh `tenant_tx` hi rasta hai. Routes ke paas helper `_tx(request, p)` hai jo `tenant_tx(sm, p.tenant_id, p.user_id)` deta hai, toh Principal se context automatic aata hai. Worker bhi `tenant_tx(sm, msg['tenant_id'])` use karta hai.

Note karo ki `app.user_id` bhi set hota hai -- original memberships policy usko OR mein use karti thi. Migration 0003 ke baad koi policy usse use nahi karti; woh ab sirf context ke liye hai (future policies/triggers ke liye available).
why_needed: Yeh function poore isolation design ka entry point hai -- interviewer chahega ki aap iska exact behaviour aur edge cases bata sako.
real_world_analogy: Office ka visitor badge printer: har meeting ke shuru mein badge pe company ka naam print hota hai, meeting khatam hone pe badge shred. Bina badge (global_tx) ke tum sirf lobby (users/tenants) mein ja sakte ho.
how_it_works: async_sessionmaker -> AsyncSession -> begin() -> set_config x2 -> yield -> commit/rollback -> connection pool mein wapas.
in_this_project: `saas/db/session.py`: `make_engine` (pool_size=10, max_overflow=10, pool_pre_ping=True), `make_sessionmaker` (expire_on_commit=False), `tenant_tx`, `global_tx`. Routes: `api/routes.py::_tx`.

    """No tenant context: tenant tables return no rows (RLS fails closed). For users/tenants/auth."""
    async with tenant_tx(sm, None, user_id) as s:
        yield s

question: Explain the per-tenant token bucket Lua script in limits.py line by line.
answer_hinglish:
`_BUCKET` Lua script Redis mein atomically chalta hai -- ek tenant ke saare API replicas ek hi bucket share karte hain aur read-modify-write ke beech koi race nahi. ARGV[1] = capacity (plan.burst), ARGV[2] = rate (plan.requests_per_second). Line by line: (1) `redis.call('TIME')` se current time ms mein -- Redis ka clock, app servers ka nahi, toh clock skew ka issue nahi. (2) `HMGET key tokens ts` -- pehli baar nil hai toh tokens = cap (full bucket), ts = now. (3) Lazy refill: `tokens = min(cap, tokens + max(now - ts, 0) * rate / 1000)` -- koi background timer nahi; jitna time beeta utne tokens add. `max(...,0)` negative elapsed se bachata hai. (4) Agar `tokens >= 1` toh ek token consume, wait = 0; warna `wait = ceil((1 - tokens) * 1000 / rate)` -- kitne ms baad ek token banega. (5) `HSET` new state. (6) `PEXPIRE` = time to fully refill + 1s, toh idle tenants ki keys khud expire. (7) `return wait`.

Python side `check_rate` wait > 0 pe `TooManyRequests` raise karta hai with `Retry-After` = ceil(wait/1000), minimum 1 second. `register_script` EVALSHA use karta hai. `RedisError` pe return -- fail open.

Test: free plan burst 10, rps 5 -- 15 rapid requests mein pehli 9 definitely 200 aur kam se kam ek 429 (`test_tenant_rate_limit_and_quota`). Note: denied request bhi state write karta hai (ts update) -- yeh theek hai kyunki tokens fractional refill already add ho chuke.
why_needed: Rate limiting distributed systems ka classic topic hai; Lua atomicity aur lazy refill samjhana senior-level signal hai.
real_world_analogy: Paani ki tanki jisme nal se fixed speed se paani aata hai (refill rate), tanki ki capacity burst hai, aur har request ek glass nikalti hai. Glass nahi bhar sakta toh 'itni der baad aana' bolte ho.
how_it_works: EVALSHA -> single-threaded Redis mein atomic execution -> HMGET/compute/HSET/PEXPIRE -> wait ms return.
in_this_project: `saas/services/limits.py::_BUCKET`, `TenantLimits.check_rate`. Key `saas:rl:{tenant_id}`. Plan values `core/plans.py`. Yeh Project 1 (rate limiter) ka idea per-tenant plan ke saath reuse hai.
code_example:
-- real (from limits.py _BUCKET)
local t = redis.call('TIME'); local now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000)
local s = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(s[1]) or cap; local ts = tonumber(s[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + math.max(now - ts, 0) * rate / 1000)
local wait = 0
if tokens >= 1 then tokens = tokens - 1 else wait = math.ceil((1 - tokens) * 1000 / rate) end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tostring(tokens), 'ts', tostring(now))
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(cap * 1000 / rate) + 1000)
return wait

Redis down -> fail open
Ek tenant ke saare users ek bucket share karte hain
common_mistakes: App ke clock se time lena
GET + SET alag commands (race)
Key pe expiry na lagana (memory leak)

Redis Cluster mein yeh script kaise chalega?
Fixed window counter se yeh better kyun?

question: How does usage metering work -- INCR in Redis, then flush_usage_to_db? Why GREATEST in the upsert?
answer_hinglish:
Hot path pe har tenant request `meter()` call karti hai: key `saas:usage:{tenant_id}:api_calls:{YYYY-MM}` pe pipeline mein `INCR` aur `EXPIRE 40 din`. Ek round trip, O(1). Naya value plan ke `monthly_api_calls` se compare -- zyada toh 429 `quota_exceeded`. Period key mein hai, toh mahina badla aur naya counter automatically start; 40 din ki expiry purane counters saaf karti hai.

Postgres mein durable record ke liye `flush_usage_to_db` hai: `scan_iter(match='saas:usage:*')` se saari keys, har key ko parse karke `tenant_id, metric, period` nikalta hai, value GET karta hai, aur us tenant ke `tenant_tx` mein upsert: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, metric, period) DO UPDATE SET value = GREATEST(usage_counters.value, EXCLUDED.value)`. Worker yeh har 60 second chalata hai; admin `/admin/tenants/{id}/usage` bhi pehle flush karta hai.

GREATEST kyun, `value + EXCLUDED.value` kyun nahi? Kyunki hum Redis ka ABSOLUTE count copy kar rahe hain, delta nahi. `+=` karte toh har flush double count karta. Absolute set idempotent hai -- flush do baar chalo, result same. Aur GREATEST (plain `= EXCLUDED.value` ki jagah) ek extra guard hai: agar Redis restart/flush ho gaya aur counter 0 se dobara shuru hua, toh Postgres ki badi value overwrite nahi hogi -- DB counter kabhi peeche nahi jaata. Har insert `tenant_tx` mein hai kyunki `usage_counters` pe RLS + FORCE hai.

Limitation (README): Redis loss = last flush ke baad ke counts gaye; aur quota Redis se hi padha jaata hai, toh Redis reset = quota bhi reset.
why_needed: Usage-based billing har modern SaaS mein hai; hot path cheap rakhna aur durable record idempotent banana -- dono samjhana zaroori.
real_world_analogy: Dukaan ka cash counter (Redis) din bhar fast count karta hai, aur har ghante manager register (Postgres) mein 'ab tak total' likhta hai -- 'aur itna jodo' nahi, taaki do baar likhne se galti na ho.
how_it_works: Request -> INCR (Redis) -> compare quota. Worker every 60s -> SCAN keys -> GET -> upsert GREATEST in tenant_tx.
in_this_project: `saas/services/limits.py::TenantLimits.meter`, `flush_usage_to_db`, `period()`. `saas/worker.py` loop mein `if time.monotonic() - last_flush > 60`. Table `usage_counters PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, metric, period)`. Test: `test_platform_admin_suspension` usage[0].metric == 'api_calls' check karta hai.

    _, _, tenant_id, metric, per = key.decode().split(":", 4)
    value = int(await self.r.get(key) or 0)
    async with tenant_tx(sm, tenant_id) as s:
        await s.execute(text(
            "INSERT INTO usage_counters (tenant_id, metric, period, value) VALUES (:t, :m, :p, :v) "
            "ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, metric, period) DO UPDATE SET value = GREATEST(usage_counters.value, EXCLUDED.value)"),
            {"t": tenant_id, "m": metric, "p": per, "v": value})
disadvantages: Redis loss = unflushed counts lost aur quota reset
Har key ka alag transaction (N round trips)
SCAN poore keyspace pe
common_mistakes: Delta add karna absolute value pe

advanced.failure_scenarios: Redis crash -> last 60s lost aur quota counter 0 se; worker down -> Postgres stale; do workers parallel flush -> GREATEST se safe.
advanced.alternatives: Kafka/stream mein usage events -> analytics store (SYSTEM_DESIGN 100x); Redis AOF everysec; Postgres batch insert of deltas with idempotency keys.

question: How is an API key authenticated, and how are its effective permissions computed?
answer_hinglish:
Flow: client `Authorization: Bearer sk_...` bhejta hai. `tenant_principal` dekhta hai ki token `API_KEY_PREFIX` ('sk_') se shuru hai. Phir `global_tx` mein `SELECT * FROM resolve_api_key(:h)` jahan `h = sha256(token)`. SECURITY DEFINER function exact hash pe `revoked_at IS NULL` wali key dhoondhta hai aur `key_id, tenant_id, scopes, created_by` deta hai. Na mile -> 401 'invalid API key'. Key ka `tenant_id` URL ke tenant se match na kare -> 404 'tenant not found' -- foreign key holder ko tenant ka existence confirm nahi karte.

Ab effective permissions: `tenant_tx` mein creator ka CURRENT role: `SELECT role FROM memberships WHERE tenant_id = :t AND user_id = :u` (u = key.created_by). Phir `perms = frozenset(P(x) for x in key.scopes) & ROLE_PERMISSIONS.get(creator_role, frozenset())`. Yeh intersection hai: key kabhi apne scopes se zyada nahi kar sakti, aur creator ke current role se bhi zyada nahi. Creator ko demote kiya -> key ki power turant ghat gayi. Creator ko tenant se hataya -> role None -> empty set -> har permission check 403.

Creation time pe bhi guard hai: `create_api_key` mein `set(body.scopes) - set(p.permissions)` non-empty ho toh 403 'scopes exceed your own permissions'. Test `test_api_keys_scoped_and_bounded_by_creator`: project:read key se GET 200, POST 403, doosre tenant pe 404, `/me` pe 401 (user-only route), revoke ke baad 401, aur admin `billing:manage` scope wali key nahi bana sakta.

API key Principal ka `role` None aur `user_id` None hota hai, `api_key_id` set -- audit mein actor key dikhti hai.
why_needed: Machine credentials har B2B SaaS mein hote hain; 'key outlives its creator's power' ek real-world vulnerability class hai.
real_world_analogy: Company ka temporary access card jo manager ne contractor ke liye banaya: card pe likhe areas (scopes) se zyada nahi khulega, aur manager ka access ghata ya manager company chhod gaya toh card bhi utna hi kam/bekaar.
how_it_works: sha256 -> resolve_api_key (definer) -> tenant match -> creator role (RLS) -> scopes INTERSECT role perms -> Principal(api_key_id).
in_this_project: `saas/api/deps.py::tenant_principal` (API key branch), `saas/services/tenancy.py::create_api_key`, `revoke_api_key`. Key raw sirf creation response mein ('shown once; only a hash is stored'); `prefix` (pehle 10 chars) identification ke liye stored. FAILURE_SCENARIOS #12.

    raise NotFound("tenant not found")   # don't confirm the tenant exists to a foreign key
async with tenant_tx(app.state.sm, tid) as s:
    creator_role = await s.scalar(text("SELECT role FROM memberships WHERE tenant_id = :t AND user_id = :u"),
                                  {"t": tid, "u": key.created_by})
# A key can't outlive its creator's power: scopes AND the creator's CURRENT role.
perms = frozenset(P(x) for x in key.scopes) & (ROLE_PERMISSIONS.get(creator_role, frozenset()))
